nameStory: The white-striped centipede gets its name from the distinctive pale or whitish stripes that run along its dark body, creating a striking contrast that helps distinguish it from other soil-dwelling centipedes. The species name 'vesuviana' hints at its original discovery near Mount Vesuvius in Italy, though this hardy little predator has since made its home in soils across the globe.
description: The white-striped centipede is a slender, worm-like predator that spends most of its life hunting in the soil beneath our feet. Unlike the fast-moving house centipedes you might see scurrying across your basement floor, this species is built for underground life with a flexible, elongated body that can squeeze through tiny soil spaces. They typically measure 1-2 inches long and have dozens of short legs that help them navigate through dirt and leaf litter. Their most striking feature is the pale striping that contrasts against their darker body segments.

idTips.label: White stripes
idTips.description: Look for distinctive pale or whitish stripes running lengthwise along a darker brown or reddish-brown body - these stripes are often the first thing you'll notice when you uncover one

idTips.label: Flexible body
idTips.description: The body feels surprisingly soft and flexible when gently touched, almost rubbery, and can coil and twist easily unlike rigid insects

idTips.label: Many short legs
idTips.description: Count dozens of pairs of short, stubby legs along the entire body length - they move in wave-like motions rather than the quick scurrying of house centipedes

idTips.label: Soil habitat
idTips.description: Found by digging in moist soil or turning over logs and rocks - they quickly try to burrow back into the earth when exposed to light

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Body is distinctly segmented like a tiny train, with each segment roughly the same width, creating an even cylindrical appearance

habitat: White-striped centipedes thrive in the rich, moist soils of New England's forests, particularly under decaying logs, leaf litter, and moss-covered rocks. They prefer areas with consistent moisture and organic matter, making them common in deciduous and mixed woodlands from the coast to mid-elevations. You'll often find them in garden soil, compost piles, and anywhere earthworms are abundant, as they share similar habitat preferences.

seasonality.spring: Most active as soil warms and becomes workable - this is the best time to find them when turning over logs or digging in garden soil. They're often closer to the surface as they hunt for newly active prey.
seasonality.summer: Present but deeper in soil during hot, dry periods - look for them in consistently moist areas like stream banks or under thick mulch. Early morning or after rain brings them closer to the surface.
seasonality.fall: Very active again as they feed heavily before winter - excellent time for observation when raking leaves or preparing garden beds. Often found concentrated under thick leaf litter.
seasonality.winter: Dormant deep in soil below frost line, rarely seen unless digging in protected areas like compost piles or greenhouses. Occasionally found under deep mulch during mild spells.

funFact: Despite being called a 'centipede' (meaning 100 feet), white-striped centipedes actually have anywhere from 54 to 354 legs depending on their age and size - and they're born with just a few pairs, growing more legs with each molt throughout their lives, like adding train cars to their body!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with earthworms when first spotted, but centipedes have distinct segments with visible legs on each section, while earthworms are smooth and legless. Remember: 'Legs = predator centipede, smooth = decomposer earthworm.'
contextualKnowledge: There's often confusion about centipede leg counts since 'centipede' literally means '100 feet,' but no centipede species actually has exactly 100 legs. Soil centipedes like this one are also completely different from the long-legged house centipedes people see indoors - they're adapted for entirely different lifestyles and habitats.
compareHints: Since this is the only Henia species commonly found in New England, compare it with other soil centipedes in the Geophilidae family by looking for the distinctive white striping - most other soil centipedes in our region are uniformly colored without contrasting stripes. The striping pattern is remarkably consistent and makes this species stand out clearly from its plain-colored relatives.
